What is this classic logical paradox called?

A class takes a test. The students who scored in the top 10% are given a harder retest the next day, and on average they score lower the second time. A teacher concludes the harder test caused the drop. Is that conclusion justified?
choices: No, because test scores are entirely random and carry no information
Yes, but only because the grading got stricter overnight
Yes — the second test was objectively harder, so it must have caused the lower scores
No — this is regression to the mean: unusually high scores tend to be followed by scores closer to average even without any real change

questions.q: During WWII, statistician Abraham Wald studied bullet-hole patterns on bombers that returned from missions: the wings and fuselage were riddled with holes, while the engines and cockpit were almost untouched. Where did he recommend adding armor?
choices: The engines and cockpit — planes hit there rarely made it back to be counted
Nowhere — the data shows these bombers were rarely hit at all
Spread the armor evenly across the whole aircraft
The wings and fuselage, since that's clearly where planes take the most hits
